Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01349

A consequence: A nature and a universal kind depend on their parts—such as broader kind and difference, or matter and form—in order to be constituted. This dependence concerns what they are in themselves, or what they are as existent. Their dependence on a maker and an end, by contrast, concerns their coming about. The first two are causes of a nature, whether considered in general or in some particular way of existing; the latter two are causes of its existence. So causation and being caused, when they mean bringing something about and coming about, apply to natures only when existence is considered together with them. This differs from causation and being constituted, which apply to a nature considered apart from whether it exists or not. This is also why knowledge involves two different tasks: judging whether a statement is true and understanding what a thing is.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01350

Ibn Sina says in The Healing, at the start of the chapter on the subject of logic: “The mind cannot move from a simple idea alone to a judgment that something is true, because that idea by itself does not determine whether the thing exists or not. A judgment must have a basis that brings it about, and nothing can serve as that basis whether it exists or not. So a simple idea does not suffice unless the thing’s existence or nonexistence—or some condition of it—is established. But we can often form a conception from a simple idea.”
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01351

Al-Dawani objected: “There is a problem here. First, the same point undermines conception, since the premises apply to it too. Second, the simple idea may bring about assent because it exists in the mind, without our first assenting to its existence there—just as it can bring about conception by itself. So Ibn Sina’s point is a fallacy, and it is strange to find it in a thinker like him.” That is what he says in his treatise A Model of the Sciences.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01352

What we have said shows why forming an idea differs from judging that a claim is true. To judge whether a claim is true, we must first establish the reasons for it. Those reasons bring about our judgment; they are not simply parts of the idea being judged. A theoretical claim is first conceived before proof is given, without conceiving its premises or assenting to them in any way. Then, after considering the claim and its premises, the mind forms the premises that prove it and moves from them to assent. In that respect, the premises are like efficient causes of a nature’s existence, or of one of its features. Bahmanyar’s words support this: “The relation of first principles to all theoretical claims is like the relation of the agent that brings about all things to the things that exist.”
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01353

A question that asks us to understand a thing—especially by defining it—depends on its near and remote principles in a different way. Its parts fit together and constitute it in meaning and nature, not by bringing it into existence. The parts of a definition stand to the thing defined in this way.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01354
This establishes the difference between accepting a claim as true and forming an idea of something. With a little thought, it also answers both objections.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01355
III. Can existence grow stronger or weaker?
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01356

Growth or decline in intensity is motion in quality, just as increase or decrease is motion in quantity. Motion in a category means that, at each imagined moment, the changing thing is in a state of that category different—in kind, type, or some other way—from its state at another moment. Some think this means that the category itself changes in its state. That is wrong. To become blacker, for example, does not mean that one and the same blackness grows stronger. That would make blackness itself the thing moving, even though the first blackness is incomplete in itself and is not the same as the stronger one.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01357

Nor can anyone say that the first state remains while something is added to it. If what is added is not blackness, then the blackness has not grown stronger in its blackness; another feature has appeared. If what is added is another blackness, two blacknesses would occupy one and the same thing, with no difference in their nature, place, or time. That is impossible. Nor can two blacknesses become one: if both remain, they have not become one. The same is true if they both disappear and a third takes their place, or if one disappears and the other remains. So blackness grows stronger not by the first blackness remaining while another is added, but by the first ceasing to exist in the thing and a stronger blackness taking its place, while the thing remains through both states. The same reasoning applies when blackness grows weaker.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01358

Once this is clear, we can see that existence itself does not move. This is obvious for those who treat existence as only a mental idea and say it multiplies only as the things that have it multiply. On our view, we have already seen that existence is not an extra feature attached to a nature. It is the thing’s very existence—its being existent—and, in reality, it is the thing itself. How could it change while what it is identical with remains unchanged, both in reality and in how it is brought about? Only when the mind views it in a certain way could it seem to change. Also, if existence itself moved, the thing in motion could not exist in a complete, actual way for as long as the motion lasted. At no point in that motion would it be fully settled in the very existence that was changing. A thing cannot change in what it depends on to exist, such as existence itself or the basic forms that make it what it is. There is another issue to consider here, which we will explain later, God willing.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01359

An objection, and a warning: If motion means what we have just described, someone may argue that nothing can change in any of these kinds of features. A subject can move from one instance to another only if those individual instances exist in reality. But they do not. If they did, one instant would have to follow another with nothing between them, and infinitely many ordered things would be confined between two limits. We can answer that, although these instances do not exist as separate actual things, they exist as near possibilities. That is, at any imagined moment, if motion stopped then, the moving subject would be in one definite instance from among them. Someone objects that this would mean a thing moving from place to place has no actual place during its motion, and a thing changing in size has no actual size. This is plainly false.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01360

Al-Dawani answers that, during motion, the changing thing exists only in the intermediate state between those instances. This state lies between mere possibility and full reality. It is enough to show that a body is never without those features or without this intermediate state. It is neither necessary nor proved that the body always has one of their instances in full reality; in fact, a proof may show the opposite. That is his view.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01361

But the problem with this view is clear. Anything moving from place to place is surrounded by a body at every moment of its motion, so it must have an actual place; otherwise, there would be a void, which is impossible. Also, the heavenly spheres are always in rotational motion, so this view would mean they never have a position at all.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01362

The truth here is that the instances of the kind in which motion takes place are not limited to momentary instances. There are momentary states, which set the standard for rest, and states that unfold gradually through time across the motion as a whole. Some thinkers say that the motion considered as a whole is itself one of these temporal states. While motion continues without a break, the changing thing has one connected state in that category. It is not at rest. It has one identity spread continuously through time, with a measurable length, and contains all the points we imagine at separate moments, just as imagined points lie along a line. This ongoing state of the category is real; we do not need to imagine or divide it for it to exist. The momentary states and the parts and limits of that ongoing state exist only because we imagine them. So the body is never without the kind of feature in which it moves. We do not need a chain of separate instants, or infinitely many actual moments between two limits: during motion, no single momentary state exists as a complete, separate thing, let alone an endless succession of such instants.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01363

Nor can you return and say that, for existence to grow stronger or weaker, it is enough that the thing remains stable. Motion requires its subject to persist, but a state that exists only in time does not persist at all—not during the time when it exists, nor beyond that time. A fuller explanation will come in our discussion of motion and time, God willing.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01364
IV. Degrees of intensity and weakness
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01365

Perhaps you have learned in your earlier studies that two things can differ, in reality or in thought, in one of three ways. They may differ in their entire essence, sharing no essential feature, as the categories do. Or they may share an essential nature but differ in one part of it: the shared nature is the broader kind, and what distinguishes each kind within it is its defining feature. Together, broader kind and defining feature make a specific nature; this is a unified kind of composition. Or they may share their whole essential nature and differ only through added accidental features. What results are individual or species-level instances, joined by those added features.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01366

But you may have overlooked a fourth kind, proposed by the Illuminationist philosophers, that breaks this three-part division. The difference may lie neither in the whole essence, nor in one part of it, nor in something added to it. Instead, one and the same nature may differ in how complete or deficient it is. It can have different levels within itself, apart from the incidental differences among the individuals that share it but also have other defining or accidental features. The two schools disagree here. Aristotle’s followers argue that this cannot be right: if the more complete thing contains nothing the less complete one lacks, the two do not differ at all. But if it does contain something the other lacks, then that feature is either part of the shared nature, in which case the two do not really share it, or an added feature, which must be either an essential defining feature or an accident.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01367

Even setting aside the problem with accidents, this argument is very weak. It assumes what it needs to prove: two things may differ in the very respect in which they agree, rather than through something added to it. Consider two instances of blackness, for example. If they differ by a defining feature, that defining feature cannot be part of the essence of blackness itself; otherwise, it would not distinguish one from the other. Rather, it would divide their shared broader kind, blackness, into two kinds. The defining feature would then lie outside the essence of that broader kind, like other accidental features. So if blackness grows stronger because of a defining feature whose meaning is not blackness, the difference lies beyond blackness itself—even though we have assumed that it lies within it.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01368

They reply that the difference among individual things belongs to a derived feature such as “black,” which is applied to things that bear blackness. Some bear an instance of blackness that is more complete at the level of its individuality; others bear a less complete one. Individuality comes from features that distinguish each thing, not from the general, still-indeterminate nature itself. So what differs is the individual identity, not the nature considered in itself. By saying that degrees belong to a derived term such as “black,” they mean that this word points both to blackness and to the thing that bears it. The bearer is one of the features that makes it an individual. Their point, then, is that the difference lies in individual identity, not in the nature itself.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01369

One might object that moving the difference to individuality does not help; it brings back the very problem they were trying to avoid. If a nature varies because of the features that make each instance an individual, the question about how the nature varies still stands. If the difference comes from the natures themselves, then the nature itself admits differences in degree. If it comes from the way the nature varies, the explanation is circular. If it comes from further individualizing features, an endless regress follows. And if individuality is existence, but existence is only a mental construct, how can it ground this difference? If existence is real, however, then it varies in itself, because the identity of an existent thing is its existence. On that view, gradation belongs to existence itself.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01370

We reply that, according to Aristotle’s followers, a nature itself—whether a substance or a feature of something else—cannot vary by degrees. A broader kind differs among its instances through defining features. These features differ in themselves, just as distinct species differ in their essences; that is a difference between kinds, not a difference of degree. Differences of degree occur within one nature, across its more and less complete levels. If it is a specific nature that differs, the variation is explained by different matter and by features that distinguish each individual. Those, in turn, may differ because of earlier matter surrounded by other features, and so on. Aristotle’s followers allow this chain to continue indefinitely, one difference following another. This is what they mean when they say that a nature differs at the level of its individuals, and that difference through accidents is like difference through defining features: the full set of features surrounding one thing differs from the full set surrounding another. That is difference between distinct instances, not gradation.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01371

As for the questioner's point that, if individuality is existence, existence itself must vary in its own nature, that is right; the author will establish it later. The Aristotle’s followers may mean that they deny gradation in an essence understood as what a thing is, but not in existence itself. Their reference to individuality may point to existence, since, strictly speaking, a nature becomes an individual only through a mode of existence. Their claim that a generic nature differs through defining features may point to the same thing: defining features are modes of existence, as the author will show. Existences and identities differ not through matter or material accidents, but in themselves, because existence is identity, and what distinguishes them is also what they share. Some of the Aristotle’s followers' statements about difference can be read as describing degrees of rank, as in al-Shawāhid al-rubūbiyya. The author's phrase “the defining features of blackness” answers the Illuminationists' objection: a defining feature is accidental to the essence of a broader kind, but not to its existence. Existence itself is one, and a broader kind is applied to a defining feature only indirectly. So a difference through defining features need not be a difference in something outside generic blackness.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01372

You can see that it is far from right to say that intense and weak blackness do not differ in their blackness, or that blackness applies to both in exactly the same way and the difference lies only between the bodies that bear them. If differences between the underlying qualities make the derived word apply differently to their subjects, then those differences should also make the quality itself apply differently to its two instances. In fact, that is the more plausible conclusion.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01373

Another argument of theirs is this: if the complete level is the essence itself, then the deficient and intermediate levels are not that same essence; and if either of those is the essence, the others are not. But this does not settle the question about a specific nature. Only numerical unity cannot be shared or vary; a nature can be one in meaning while appearing at different levels. The other side can say that the specific nature is what all three levels share: the more complete, the less complete, and the intermediate.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01374

You may reply that, if the natural universal exists outside the mind, then the feature shared by all three levels also exists outside the mind, even though the mind is where we recognize them as sharing it. Once the mind strips away added and individualizing features, what remains must match the complete level or one of the less complete levels. Either way, it cannot match all of them. It would account for only one level, leaving the others to depend on something outside the shared nature. That contradicts the assumption that this nature is common to them all.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01375

I answer that the natural universal, as you understand it, applies only to natures whose instances are alike in every essential respect. Only natures that apply in exactly the same way to every instance meet that condition. Once we set aside the added features, the nature is the same in every case, with no difference of degree. A gradable nature is different. Each level that exists in the world—in one individual or in several—would, if considered by the mind, be understood at that very level once its external features were stripped away. The same is true of every other level. These levels, taken from actual individuals and represented in the mind, are not equally complete or deficient. So none of them is universal in a way that applies to every individual across all the levels. They do share one underlying nature, but it is utterly indeterminate. It is indeterminate in its own completeness and deficiency, beyond the vagueness that comes from differences among individuals in their identities.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01376

A detailed clarification: The general rule for graded difference, in all its forms, is this: a universal nature applies to its individuals with greater claim, priority, or completeness. Greater completeness includes greater intensity, size, or number. The earlier Shi‘i philosophers and the Aristotle’s followers who followed Aristotle disagreed on four questions. The first is whether an essence, or an essential feature, can vary among its instances by any kind of gradation—by having a greater claim, coming earlier or later, or being more or less complete—or whether this is impossible. Some later philosophers have claimed that it is self-evident and universally agreed that essential natures cannot vary in the first two ways. This is highly doubtful. They seem to have overlooked that, for the Persian and earlier philosophers, some luminous substances are causes of others through their simple substantial nature.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01377

The second question is whether stronger and weaker degrees must belong to different kinds. In other words, must the difference between them come from their essential features, so that they differ in species? Or can some instances share the same species, even if all do not? The third question is whether differences in quality and quantity are two kinds of gradation or one, even if we use different comparative words for them. The fourth is whether strength and weakness, completeness and deficiency, occur only in quantity and quality or also in other kinds of thing, such as substance. Philosophers in Aristotle’s school chose the first option in each question; the Stoics chose the second. Let us take them one by one.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01378

As for the first question: you know by now that existence is one reality. It has no broader kind or defining feature, and it has the same meaning in all things. Its real instances do not differ through essences separate from one another, nor through identities separate from their essences; their identities are their essences. We have also seen that making and being made belong only to actual existences, not to universal natures. So conclude that the individual instances of existence, each made distinct by its own identity while sharing one reality, differ from one another in all the ways that gradation allows: one can have greater or lesser priority, come earlier or later, or be stronger or weaker.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01379

One clue is that the parts of time are alike in kind, yet one comes before another by its own nature, not because of some outside feature. The Illuminationist Shaykh offers another proof in al-Muṭāraḥāt. He argues that a greater and a lesser quantity do not differ because of an added accident or a defining feature that divides quantity. The difference between quantities lies in quantity itself: what one has beyond the other is not outside quantity, but belongs to the same nature they share. A longer and a shorter line differ only in how complete or incomplete they are as lines. The same is true of more and less complete blackness: they share blackness, and their difference comes from no feature outside blackness itself. It lies in blackness.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01380

The reply is that a longer and a shorter line have one and the same nature. Their difference is not in quantity itself, even though it occurs within quantity. What makes the difference is not the shared nature in which the difference occurs. Instead, each line has its own particular extent as an individual: it stretches over a certain length between set limits. This depends on differences in the matter’s readiness and its responses, so it lies outside the nature of quantity. Viewed simply as lines, the longer and shorter ones are both lengths in the same sense: each is one dimension, and neither is more of a line than the other. Compared with each other, however, the longer line is longer only in relation to the shorter one, because of its particular extent. As Avicenna says in The Categories of The Healing: “I do not mean that one quantity cannot be greater or smaller than another. I mean that one cannot be more of a quantity than another quantity like it, though it can be greater in a relative sense—that is, longer in relation to the other.”
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01381

So length itself cannot be greater or less; only relative length can. The same applies to number. Avicenna also says that number is multiplicity without comparison, while being “more numerous” is a relative feature of number. The same applies to blackness and heat: their basic nature is the same across instances, and the differences come from individual features, not from the shared nature itself. True blackness cannot be stronger or weaker in itself. What is black in relation to one thing may be white in relation to another. An instance of blackness, considered on its own, is not stronger or weaker; it becomes so only when compared. In this view, the opposition between the two extremes also extends to the intermediate shades, without creating a new kind of opposition.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01382

On this account, “stronger” or “greater” means that, with help from imagination, the mind can compare one individual with another and allow for more of the same kind to be added. It does not mean that the shared nature itself grows or that its effects appear more fully in some individuals. Otherwise, many essential natures would admit degrees: people differ, for example, in how many effects their humanity produces. Aristotle’s followers say that such differences are not differences in degree within the shared nature; they only make a derived description apply differently to the things that bear the quality. In the end, they explain the difference as one thing being more fittingly described than another. They therefore say that the two instances of blackness do not themselves differ in the feature being measured. Each has its own defining feature, which makes it the kind of blackness it is. The difference lies instead between the two bodies described as deeply or faintly black: the word “black” applies more fully to one than to the other.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01383

On this account, the Illuminationist Shaykh’s objection in al-Muṭāraḥāt does not apply. He says that those who call stronger blackness different from weaker blackness by a defining feature must treat blackness as a broader kind that admits degrees. But they also say that no broader kind admits degrees. Their objection assumes that stronger and weaker blackness differ in kind. Our account denies that.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01384

As for the second question, the Stoics and other early philosophers are right, for the same reasons we gave about the reality of existence. Existence is not made up of instances that differ in kind. Some instances are extremely strong and great; others, such as motion, prime matter, and number, are very weak. Aristotle’s followers also accept that qualities grow stronger or weaker as a physical subject moves through different levels of heat, blackness, and other qualities. They hold that one motion is a single process, with an unbroken identity from its beginning to its end. The parts and boundaries of that continuous process belong to the same species, a point they treat as self-evident in their argument against Democritus’ account of the basic parts of bodies. It follows that the strong and weak stages of blackness, as a body grows darker, are of the same species.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01385

An intensifying process may end in something different in kind from what it has passed through. But that new thing differs because it is where the process begins or ends, not because it is one of the levels through which the process moves. It may still have stronger and weaker levels of its own. Red, for example, lies between black and white. Common sense tells us that it is neither weak black nor weak white, yet red itself can be darker or lighter.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01386

As for the third question, “stronger” and “weaker” can mean what people usually mean by these words, as shown by forms such as “blacker.” The original Arabic meaning of “strong” was the power to resist; it later came to mean a greater degree of something. In everyday speech, we do not say that one line is “more of a line” than another, as we say that one blackness is “blacker” than another. So, if we judge only by common usage, strength and weakness seem to apply only to qualities, not to quantities or other things. Quantities, it seems, accept only increase or decrease, more or less.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01387

But philosophers cannot settle questions of reason by relying only on words or on everyday speech. The common-language argument is not sound even on its own terms. People may not say that one line is “more of a line” than another, but they do say that one is longer. Length is part of what it means to be a line, so strength or weakness can be found in the line itself. People also say that one line is longer or bigger than another, even though they agree that a line is a quantity.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01388

The same point applies to number. People may not say that one number is “more of a number” than another, but they do say that one number is greater. Since number and multiplicity are the same, being greater is a kind of strength in number; the reverse applies to being smaller. Some distinguish strength from increase by saying that strength has a limit, while length and number can always increase: no longest line or greatest number can be imagined, but blackness and heat might reach a point beyond which nothing could be stronger. First, we can deny that qualities have such an absolute limit, even if every quality that exists has a finite degree. The same is true of length and number: among actual examples, there may be no longer line or greater number. So this does not distinguish them.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01389

Second, even if we accept that some kinds have a limit and others do not, that still does not separate strength from increase. Either kind can have forms that stop at a limit and forms that do not; that is a further division, made after we have already divided things into stronger and weaker. Another proposed difference is that increase applies when we can point to an equal part and an extra part, while strength and weakness do not work that way. But this fails for number. A number is made of units, not of other numbers. Four is not made of three, and three is not made of two. Each whole number is a simple kind, not a sum of lower numbers. If we split four in thought, its form disappears and another number takes its place. Which part of four matches three, and which part is extra? How can we identify what is equal and what differs between simple kinds of number?
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01390

They also say that differences in quality, length, and number deserve different names because the extra part works differently in each case. In length, we can imagine a piece of the longer line that matches the shorter line, with another piece left over. In number, the extra units belong to a whole number that differs in kind and existence from the smaller number. In a quality such as blackness, however, the whole stronger reality—not a separate piece within it—is what is greater. This explanation works only if the nature shared by stronger and weaker qualities is a broader kind, and each level becomes a distinct kind through a defining feature. Then one whole nature would be stronger by its own identity, not because a separate part, real or imagined, sets it apart.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01391

Strength and weakness therefore depend on differences between the natures of things. So do “more” and “fewer,” though with the distinction already explained. Increase and decrease, by contrast, follow from differences among individual instances and their particular identities. We can grant people the usual terminology: call greater or lesser length “increase” and “decrease,” greater or smaller numbers “more” and “fewer,” and degrees in other qualities “strength” and “weakness.” All these terms share one idea: more or less completeness in the very feature being compared.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01392

As for the fourth question, early philosophers such as Empedocles and Plato taught that the substances of this lower world are shadows of the substances in the higher world. By this they meant that the lower substances are effects of the higher ones, as an object casts a shadow. The cause comes before the effect in its reality as a substance. This follows from the principle of causation and from the view that existence is the reality things have outside the mind. A cause’s priority in its nature as a substance points to greater completeness and independence. If an effect gets its substantial nature from its cause, it cannot be equally complete in that respect; the cause must be more complete. This is what “strength” means here. So one substance can be more fully a substance than another, whether or not everyday speech has a word for it. Reality is not limited by common usage.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01393

This is what the Illuminationist Shaykh means in al-Talwīḥāt when he says that all the early philosophers held that the substances of this world are shadows of those in the higher world. How, he asks, could they be equal in substantiality?
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01394

He then raises an objection: priority and strength are usually said of opposites. Substance has no opposite, so nothing can be prior or stronger in substance. He answers that necessary and higher existence is more complete and stronger than possible and caused existence. By “strength” he does not mean the power to resist, but greater completeness. These levels do not take turns in one subject; they are not opposites, and they are not stages in one process.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01395

In Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, he adds that philosophers define an animal as a body with a soul that senses and moves by choice. An animal whose soul has greater power to move and more senses has fuller powers of sensing and movement. Human animality, for example, is more complete than a mosquito’s. The fact that everyday speech does not call one animal “more animal” than another is no reason to deny the difference. Claims such as “this is not more watery than that” rest on everyday speech, not on proof.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01396

Someone may object that an animal’s defining feature is not actual sensation and movement, but the powers behind them. Actual actions differ because of the animal’s organs, its readiness to act, and the presence or removal of obstacles. The power itself does not differ. In the same way, water’s defining feature is not the coldness we feel, since that can sometimes be absent, but its power to become cold when nothing prevents it.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01397

I agree that these actions and effects are signs of the powers that define the thing, and can stand in for them in a definition. The effects arise from those powers, which is why we use them when defining things, just as we include building in the definition of a builder. More effects show a stronger power; fewer show a weaker one.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01398

A definition can describe a thing in itself, describe its relation to something else, or do both in different ways. We can define a ruler or a builder by what each is, or by the kingdom each rules or the building each builds. In a definition based on relation, the kingdom or building is included; in a definition of what the person is in himself, it is not. These two kinds of definition can come apart.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01399

The same applies to the soul. Its body and the way it governs the body are included in a definition of the soul as a manager, not in a definition of its inner nature alone. If a thing’s inner nature can be separated from its role, as with souls that do not depend on bodies, its definition by nature differs from its definition by action. But if a thing’s own being is identical with its relation or action—as with some powers and souls whose reality is to move or relate to something—then the two definitions are the same.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01400

A definition of a power through its relation must include whatever it acts on. Just as many acts of building show that someone is a more complete builder, many acts of guidance show that a soul is more complete in its role of governing.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01401

With this in place, consider souls and powers whose nature and actions depend on matter. Their existence in themselves is identical with their existence in relation to what they act on; neither the mind nor the world can separate the two. So their definition in one respect is also their definition in the other. Aristotle’s followers themselves admit that the actions of a power belong in its definition. As we have seen, more actions show a stronger active power. For the powers we are discussing, this active aspect is identical with their inner nature. These same powers are the essential features that make natural bodies different kinds. The bodies differ through their powers and forms, not through the bodily nature they all share. So when these powers differ in completeness as substances, the kinds of bodies differ as well. This is what we wanted to show.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01402

A further question and response: philosophers in Aristotle’s school ask how their rule can stand when substances cause other substances, matter and form bring about a body, and a father causes a son, even though “substance” is a broader kind shared by all of them. The same problem appears in quantity: a body comes before a surface, and a surface before a line, even though “quantity” is a broader kind that applies to all three.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01403

They answer that priority and posteriority within one concept can work in two ways. In the first, the thing that comes first and the feature in which it comes first are the same. For example, the existence of the Necessary Being comes before the existence of a possible being, and the existence of a substance before the existence of an accident. In the second, the thing that is prior and the feature that explains its priority are different. A human father is earlier than a human son, not in their shared humanity, but in another respect: their existence or the time of their birth. What differs is the time or existence; what accounts for the difference is their individual identity.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01404

With this distinction, we can see that one individual does not cause or precede another simply through its own nature, nor does it make the other an instance of the same kind by means of that nature. Cause and effect, and what is prior or later, depend on their existence, not on their essences. Existence applies first to matter and form, then to the body made from them; it also applies first to parents, then to their child. In the same way, existence applies first to substances in the higher world: they are more fully present and established than the substances in our world. But the nature “substance” applies equally to all of them. One is not more of a substance than another; one is more fully real in its existence. One existence can be naturally prior to another without any added feature. Matter and form are prior to a body in existence, not in substantial nature. The body is a substance, and so are its parts; none is more of a substance than the others. The same reasoning applies to quantity and other cases of this kind. Yet this reply faces several objections.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01405

One objection is that this answer repeats the problem it was meant to avoid. Moving the difference from substance or quantity to existence or time does not help, because the same question then applies to existence and time. If one existence is prior to another because of existence itself, then instances of one simple reality differ in priority. We have already shown that existence is one simple reality, not divided into kinds by defining features. Likewise, if parts of time come before one another because time itself is a process of renewal and passing away, then a single reality has degrees of priority and posteriority.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01406

Another objection is that the answer conflicts with their argument against one body causing the existence of another. They say that the matter of a cause comes before the body it forms, and that body comes before the matter of its effect. But the matter in the effect is of the same kind as the matter in the cause. It would follow that the effect’s matter comes before the cause’s body, so that something comes before itself. If they accept the same kind of priority in other cases of substance, however, this argument against one body causing another no longer works.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01407

The argument may apply to causes that bring existence about, such as an active or final cause, but not to causes that make up a thing, such as matter and form. A body’s essence is made from the essences of matter and form, not from their existence. If its parts were not substances, the whole would not be a substance. Just as bodyhood is said of a human through the animal nature, and animal nature is said of a human, we can say that substance is said of a body through its two parts. This needs a closer look.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01408

To see the point, distinguish parts of essence from parts of existence. Taken without any further condition, parts are parts of essence; taken as separate things, they are parts of existence. The first are broader kind and defining feature; the second are matter and form. If the parts of a body are taken as broader kind and defining feature, their substantiality comes before the body’s, but this is not gradation: in this respect, they are not separate kinds of substance from the body. If they are taken as matter and form, they are different from the body, but in this respect they do not make up its essence; they make up its existence. So what differs and comes first is existence, not substantiality.
Stage Three: What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01409
